questions.q: A continuous random variable X follows N(50, 25). What is the Z-score corresponding to X = 55? State the formula used and the numerical value.
questions.a: Z = (X - μ)/σ = (55 - 50)/5 = 1.0. A wrong answer (e.g., using variance 25 instead of SD 5 giving Z=0.2, or forgetting to subtract μ) reveals the student confuses variance (σ²) with standard deviation (σ) in the denominator, or treats Z-score as just (X/σ) without centering at the mean. This is the #1 error in board exams: mixing up σ and σ².

questions.q: Two students, A and B, take different exams. A scores 82 on Exam 1 (μ=70, σ=8). B scores 90 on Exam 2 (μ=75, σ=12). Who performed better *relative to their own exam cohort*? Explain using Z-scores without calculating exact percentiles.
questions.a: Z_A = (82-70)/8 = 1.5; Z_B = (90-75)/12 = 1.25. Since Z_A > Z_B, Student A performed better relative to their cohort. A wrong answer (e.g., comparing raw scores 90 > 82 and saying B did better) reveals the student doesn't grasp that Z-score *standardizes* for different means and spreads — the core purpose of standardization. They're comparing apples to oranges.

questions.q: The life of a ceiling fan (in days) is normally distributed with mean 300 and SD 50. Find the probability that a randomly selected fan lasts *at most* 365 days. Show the standardization step and the Z-table lookup logic.
questions.a: X ~ N(300, 50²). P(X ≤ 365) = P(Z ≤ (365-300)/50) = P(Z ≤ 1.3). From Z-table, P(Z < 1.30) = 0.9032. So probability ≈ 90.32%. A wrong answer (e.g., using 365/50 = 7.3, or looking up 1.3 in the "area from 0 to Z" table instead of "cumulative from -∞") reveals confusion between Z-table formats or missing the standardization step. NCERT uses cumulative from -∞ tables.

questions.q: In a normal distribution, 31% of items are below 45 and 8% are above 64. Find μ and σ. (Hint: Use symmetry and Z-table inverse lookup.)
questions.a: P(X < 45) = 0.31 ⇒ Z₁ = -0.50 (since P(Z < -0.50) ≈ 0.3085). P(X > 64) = 0.08 ⇒ P(X < 64) = 0.92 ⇒ Z₂ = 1.41 (since P(Z < 1.41) ≈ 0.9207). Equations: (45-μ)/σ = -0.50 and (64-μ)/σ = 1.41. Solving: subtract first from second: 19/σ = 1.91 ⇒ σ ≈ 9.95. Then μ = 45 + 0.50×9.95 ≈ 49.97. A wrong answer (e.g., using Z=+0.50 for the first equation) reveals misunderstanding that 31% < 50% means the value is *below* the mean, so Z must be negative.

questions.q: A coaching institute claims their students' JEE scores follow N(180, 30²). You suspect the true mean is lower. You test 40 random students and get sample mean 172. Can you use a Z-test here? Justify *each* condition from NCERT (sample size, independence, random selection, equal sample sizes).
questions.a: Yes, Z-test is applicable: (i) n=40 > 30 ✓, (ii) scores of different students are independent ✓, (iii) random selection stated ✓, (iv) single sample so "equal sample sizes" condition is vacuously satisfied/not applicable ✓. A wrong answer (e.g., saying "no because population SD is unknown" — but here σ=30 *is given*) reveals confusion between Z-test (σ known) and t-test (σ unknown). NCERT Z-test assumes σ is known.

questions.q: Create a real-world Indian scenario (not exams or fan lifetimes) where a normal distribution is a reasonable model. Define X, estimate plausible μ and σ, and write a probability question requiring P(a < X < b) that a Class 12 student could solve using Z-tables.
questions.a: Example: X = weight of 1kg wheat flour packets from a mill. μ = 1000g, σ = 5g (machine precision). Question: "What percentage of packets weigh between 992g and 1007g?" Solution: Z₁ = (992-1000)/5 = -1.6, Z₂ = (1007-1000)/5 = 1.4. P = P(Z<1.4) - P(Z<-1.6) = 0.9192 - 0.0548 = 0.8644 ≈ 86.4%. A poor answer (e.g., discrete counts like "number of rotis") reveals failure to distinguish continuous vs discrete random variables — a prerequisite from c12_app_cbse_06_007.
